title: Technical analysis for stockbrokers
subtitle: Support, resistance and moving averages - the simplest tools for forming a market view
openingOptions: Analysing the financial statements of companies listed on the exchange
Analysing price and volume on a chart in order to forecast the price trend
Analysing the technical condition of machinery and equipment
Using AI to forecast future prices with 100% accuracy
explanation: Technical analysis reads price and volume on a chart to identify the trend along with areas of support and resistance. It does not tell you what a business is worth - that is the job of fundamental analysis - it tells you how the market is behaving towards that stock. The single most important thing when using it is accepting that every signal is only a probability, so the stop-loss has to be set before the trade is entered rather than decided after the price has moved against you.

realWorldExample.description: An investor sees the VN-Index break through 1300 (the old resistance) on heavy volume → technical analysis points to an uptrend ahead. The broker will issue a 'BUY' so the client can join the early part of the move.

quiz.question: What are support and resistance?
options: Support: the 50-day average price; resistance: the 200-day one
Support: an area of heavy volume; resistance: an area of light volume
Support: the floor price set by the exchange for the session
Support: where price tends to bounce; resistance: where it tends to stall
quiz.explanation: Technical analysis reads price and volume on a chart to identify the trend along with areas of support and resistance. It does not tell you what a business is worth - that is the job of fundamental analysis - it tells you how the market is behaving towards that stock. The single most important thing when using it is accepting that every signal is only a probability, so the stop-loss has to be set before the trade is entered rather than decided after the price has moved against you.

quiz.question: What is a moving average (MA)?
options: The average price over the last N sessions, rolling through time
The average price weighted by the trading volume of each session
A line joining the peaks and troughs of price over a period
The price at which the majority of investors are holding positions
quiz.explanation: MA 50: the average price over the last 50 days. MA 200: the average over the last 200 days. When the MA 50 crosses above the MA 200 you get a golden cross (a buy signal); when the MA 50 crosses below the MA 200 you get a death cross (a sell signal). It is a plain average, not a volume-weighted one and not a line drawn through the highs and lows - and it says nothing about where holders actually bought.

quiz.question: At what level is the RSI (Relative Strength Index) considered 'overbought'?
options: Above 50
Above 70
Above 80
Above 100
quiz.explanation: RSI above 70 = overbought → the stock may reverse downwards. RSI below 30 = oversold → it may reverse upwards. RSI between 30 and 70 is the normal zone. The 50 line is simply the midpoint of the range and marks momentum direction rather than an extreme, 80 is a stricter threshold some traders prefer but is not the convention, and the RSI is bounded at 100 so it can never exceed that.

quiz.question: You enter at 1,250, stop at 1,200, target 1,350. What is the risk-to-reward ratio?
options: 2:1 (dividing the profit by the risk)
1:3 (measured from the stop to the target)
1:2 (risk of 50, profit of 100)
1:1 (risk of 50, profit of 50)
quiz.explanation: The risk is 50 and the expected profit is 100, which is 1:2. At that ratio you only need to be right about 40% of the time to break even - which is exactly why the structure of the trade matters more than the hit rate. Measuring from the stop to the target (150) confuses the span of the trade with the two legs either side of the entry.

quiz.question: Why are moving average crossover signals inherently lagging?
options: Because they only update once per trading session
Because the exchange publishes its data behind real time
Because they need enough volume before they confirm
Because they are computed from past price data
quiz.explanation: An average is a function of the past, so by construction the signal arrives after the move has begun. This is the inherent trade-off: the longer the averaging window, the less noisy the signal and the later it comes. Publication delay is not the issue - the data arrives in real time - the calculation does not wait on volume, and updating intraday would not remove the lag either.

keyTakeaways: TA analyses price & volume on a chart to identify the trend
Support: the floor (a level price does not fall through); resistance: the ceiling (a level it does not rise through)
MA 50/200: moving averages, used to identify the longer-term trend
TA is never 100% accurate, only a higher probability → combine it with risk management

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Pick one stock you like. Draw support & resistance on the daily chart. Compute the MA 50 & MA 200. On that basis, write one BUY/SELL recommendation with a target and a stop loss.
application.secondary: If you work as a broker, this is how you advise a client professionally instead of going on gut feel.

sections.text: Technical analysis is not 100% accurate, but it improves your odds over guessing. For a broker, that is the difference between professional advice and guesswork.

items: Support & resistance: floor & ceiling - the key levels where buying or selling volume is heavy
Moving average (MA): the rolling average - helps identify the longer-term trend
RSI (Relative Strength Index): measures how overbought or oversold a stock is

sections.text: Golden cross: the MA 50 (short term) crosses above the MA 200 (long term) → a strong buy signal, an uptrend is about to begin. Death cross: the MA 50 crosses below the MA 200 → a strong sell signal, a downtrend is about to begin. These are signals brokers use very widely when advising clients.
TA + risk management = the formula that works

TA is not 100% accurate; there is always a chance of being wrong. So every BUY recommendation has to come with a target (the price objective) and a stop loss (where you cut if you are wrong). **Example:** 'BUY at 1250, target 1300 (profit of 50), stop loss 1200 (loss of 50)' → risk equals reward, a risk/reward ratio of 1:1 (an even bet).

example.title: A worked example
example.explanation: Risking 50 to aim at 100. At that ratio you only need to be right about 40% of the time to break even - which is why risk management matters more than the hit rate. A 2:1 ratio, by contrast, requires being right more than two thirds of the time simply to avoid losing money.

sections.text: Four limitations to state plainly to the client

items: A technical signal describes past price behaviour; it is not a promise about the future. Every signal has a failure rate.
Moving average crossovers lag by construction - they confirm a trend that has already formed rather than predicting where it starts.
Illiquid stocks give markedly less reliable signals, because a handful of large orders is enough to create a false pattern.
A strong enough fundamental event - results, a change of management, a sector development - can invalidate every support and resistance level in a single session.

sections.label: Professional responsibility
sections.text: A recommendation given to a client needs a reasonable basis and must suit that particular client's circumstances and risk appetite, not rest on a single signal on a chart. The same signal can be right for someone experienced with money to spare and entirely wrong for a beginner committing most of their savings.

Finally, every recommendation should be written down: the reason for entering, the target, the stop loss and the basis for each of those numbers. It is both professional discipline and the only way to look back later and know where you went wrong - the original view, the choice of entry, or failing to honour the stop you had already set.
